records.real_world_identity_notes: The Assetto Corsa (original, non-EVO) internal id ks_alfa_romeo_gta and telemetry name "Alfa Romeo GTA" belong to Kunos Simulazioni's Dream Pack 1 DLC, which also ships the Alfa Romeo 4C and the Alfa Romeo 155 Ti V6 '93 already curated separately (alfa-romeo-155-v6-ti-1993). Kunos's own car description for this content states an Autodelta-developed, "Alleggerita" (lightweight) Giulia-based homologation special with aluminium outer body panels, magnesium alloy wheels, clear plastic (Plexiglas) side windows, roughly 750 kg dry weight, up to 170 bhp in race trim, and European Touring Car Championship titles in 1966 (Andrea de Adamich) and 1970. That is an exact match to the real car already curated in this database as the 1965 Alfa Romeo Giulia Sprint 1600 GTA (FIA homologation number 1395, dated 2 August 1965), which Assetto Corsa EVO's separate "Alfa Romeo Giulia Sprint GTA" content already maps to. Do not confuse this with the GTA 1300 Junior (smaller-displacement, lower-power sibling), the later 1750/2000 Giulia GTAm, or the unrelated 1990s-2000s Alfa Romeo 155 GTA / 156 GTA road-trim nameplates, none of which match Kunos's stated specification or the 1965-1970 competition history.
records.confidence_basis: Kunos's own Dream Pack 1 content description for ks_alfa_romeo_gta (Autodelta build, "Alleggerita" lightweight construction, aluminium panels, magnesium wheels, Plexiglas windows, ~750 kg dry weight, 170 bhp race trim, 1966 and 1970 championship titles) matches the already-curated 1965 Giulia Sprint 1600 GTA record's homologation identity and real-world notes field for field. The Steam Dream Pack 1 storefront confirms this is genuine first-party Kunos content bundled with two other exact-identity cars, ruling out a third-party or ambiguously-named mod as the source of this observation.

records.specification_basis: The existing record establishes five forward gears; Kunos's own content description independently states a 5-speed manual transmission. The existing record establishes a fully synchronised five-speed gearbox from manufacturer and exact-model technical sources; nothing in this AC observation contradicts it. The existing record establishes an H-pattern lever shifter for this car; the staged AC observation's h-pattern behavior is consistent simulator-layer confirmation, not the basis for the real-car claim. Derived from the already-established H-pattern manual gearbox mechanism: a driver-shifted gearbox must be declutched to pull away from rest, independent of this AC observation. Derived from the already-established fully synchronised gearbox construction: synchronisers match shaft speeds themselves, so a downshift blip eases the shift and settles the car without being required for the gear to engage. This follows from the existing record's construction finding and is independent of this AC observation. The reviewed sources did not establish the remaining technique and wheel fields, which stay unknown in the real-car baseline: /authentic_controls/transmission/shift_pattern, /authentic_controls/transmission/upshift/clutch, /authentic_controls/transmission/upshift/throttle_lift, /authentic_controls/transmission/upshift/automatic_cut, /authentic_controls/transmission/upshift/manual_blip, /authentic_controls/transmission/upshift/automatic_blip, /authentic_controls/transmission/downshift/clutch, /authentic_controls/transmission/downshift/throttle_lift, /authentic_controls/transmission/downshift/automatic_cut, /authentic_controls/transmission/downshift/automatic_blip, /authentic_controls/steering/wheel_rim/shape, /authentic_controls/steering/wheel_rim/integrated_display, /authentic_controls/steering/wheel_rim/open_top, /authentic_controls/steering/wheel_rim/shift_lights.
